title: People are a thicket
hook: an elephant trainer says animals are easy to read, people a tangle

segments.voice: Yesterday: get out, Mara, and your line, I see you. When a mood moved in, did you stop and name it? Day four hundred forty-three.

Dog people will tell you a dog can't lie. When it's happy, the whole back half wags. When it's guilty, it can't meet your eyes. People are harder. A smile can mean anything. A yes can mean no. A fine can mean please ask again. A son of an elephant trainer named Pessa once sat with the Buddha and said exactly this, from long experience with animals much bigger than dogs. Today: people are a thicket.
screen: `A DOG CAN'T LIE.` → `A SMILE CAN MEAN ANYTHING.` → `PESSA, THE ELEPHANT TRAINER'S SON.`

segments.voice: This is the fifty-first discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the discourse to Kandaraka, a wanderer who came along with Pessa. Pessa says something honest. People are a tangle, a thicket. Animals are an open clearing. I can train an elephant, he says, and in the time it takes to go to the town and back, it will show me every trick and dodge it has. But the people who work in my house do one thing with their bodies, say another thing with their words, and have something else again in their minds. The Buddha agrees: that's so, Pessa. People are a thicket. Then he offers a way to see through the tangle, not by reading faces, but by watching what people do to themselves and to others. There are four kinds of people. One torments himself: harsh practices that hurt only his own body. One torments others: the hunter, the butcher, the jailer, the one whose living is other people's pain. One torments both: a king, say, who holds a great sacrifice that exhausts himself and drives his servants with sticks and fear. And one torments neither: who lives, here and now, cool and at peace. Pessa is delighted and leaves early, with somewhere to be. The Buddha says: if he had stayed a little longer, he would have gained a great deal. We all know Pessa's problem. People are hard to read. But the Buddha's answer isn't to become a better mind reader. It's to look at the harm and the ease people bring, and to ask which of the four we are becoming ourselves.
screen: `PEOPLE ARE A TANGLE; ANIMALS ARE OPEN` · `BODY, WORDS AND MIND DON'T MATCH` · `FOUR KINDS: WHO DO THEY TORMENT?` · `THE ONE WHO TORMENTS NEITHER` · then, large: `PEOPLE ARE THICKETS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one person gently. Think of someone who confuses you: what they say doesn't match what they do. Sit, and don't try to solve them. Just ask the Buddha's question, softly: where is the pain in their life, toward themselves, toward others? Let some compassion for the tangle come up. Then turn the question once toward yourself, without blame. Then rest with the breath, open as a clearing. The bell holds the time.
gahana. An elephant trainer's son's honest line: animals are open, people are tangled. The Buddha agrees, and offers four kinds of people to read by. Today's word.
Your line: people are thickets. Today, when someone's words and actions don't match, give them the patience you'd give a tangle, and watch what they do. Day four hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use MN 51's four kinds of persons to reflect on harm and harmlessness, and to point to the person who torments neither self nor others as the ideal of the path.

fork.setup: you're Pessa. the Buddha has begun describing four kinds of people, and you're delighted. but you have somewhere to be. what happens in the story?
options: he asks to become a monk.
fork.reveal: Pessa leaves early. after he goes, the Buddha tells the monks that if Pessa had stayed a little longer, he would have gained a great deal.

original.note: Pali gahana: a thicket, a tangle. people, Pessa says, are gahana.

trapdoor: what you thought: some people are just hard to figure out, and that's that.
what it means: look past faces to what people do: whom they harm, and whether they've found ease.
what a scholar hears: the fourth kind, who torments neither, is described in MN 51 by the full gradual training, ending in a person 'cooled' (sitibhuta), a word for the peace of nibbana.
recall: a lion's roar: a bold claim

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 51, Kandaraka Sutta (the discourse to Kandaraka)

notes: MN 51 paraphrased: Pessa's comparison (people a thicket/tangle, animals open), the elephant showing its tricks in the time it takes to go to Campa and back, workers' body/speech/mind mismatch, the four kinds of persons, Pessa leaving early. Confirm.
The sutta's 'slaves, messengers and servants' is softened to 'the people who work in my house'; confirm acceptable.
Trapdoor: sitibhuta as the 'cooled' state: confirm.
